cGLO0v5OaDc.title: Tafsir of Surat Al-Saffat, Part 6: Verses 99-113
cGLO0v5OaDc.one_line: Ibrahim's sacrifice of his son as the surah's centrepiece: forty years awaiting a dua, a command he never questioned, and why Allah never commands harm.
cGLO0v5OaDc.summary: He calls the sacrifice the main story of the surah, relived every year in Hajj, and explains that the Quran retells stories from different angles, detailing in each surah the part that serves its theme. After the fire, Ibrahim emigrates from his native land and asks for a righteous child, the dua every parent should make, since a child who strays is a lasting heartbreak. Some forty years pass between that dua and the good news of a forbearing son, so we should not be impatient or forget the duas we made. He recounts Hajar and Ismail left beside the Kaaba, which predates Ibrahim, the spring of Zamzam and the Jurhum who settled there, and argues that all of Ibrahim's descendants, Arabs included, are Hebrews, so expelling Palestinians to make room for 'the Hebrews' is absurd. When the son came of age, Ibrahim saw the same vision three nights in a row. The Quran's great arguer and critical thinker raised no objection here, and Ismail answered that his father should do as commanded. That is the meaning of aslama, full submission, though one must first be certain that something truly is Allah's command. They rejected Shaytan at the places now marked by the jamarat, the blade struck without cutting, and a ram ransomed the boy. Because the act had no benefit, it never happened: Allah tests submission but never commands harm, which Eid celebrates.

outline.heading: Opening
The main story of the surah, relived in Hajj
outline.gist: Most of Hajj traces Ibrahim's steps in this story, in which he receives an unthinkable command.

outline.heading: Each surah tells the part of the story it needs
outline.gist: Nuh's defence is detailed in one surah and the ship and his son in Hud; this is the only place the sacrifice is told.

outline.heading: Subtle differences are purposeful
outline.gist: Noticing what is added or left out across retellings reveals what Allah wants us to focus on.

outline.heading: 'I am going to my Lord': emigrating from Babylon
outline.gist: Saved from the fire, Ibrahim had to leave Babylon because he was no longer welcome.

outline.heading: The dua for a righteous child
outline.gist: Every parent's dua, because a child who goes their own way is a heartbreak one never gets over.

outline.heading: Forty years between two verses
outline.gist: Thirty seconds of recitation spans four decades; humans want answers now, but a forbearing son came to a patient father.

outline.heading: Sarah, Hajar and the order of the sons
outline.gist: Sarah bore Ishaq only in old age; Ismail came from Hajar, met in Egypt, after travels through Sham and Palestine.

outline.heading: Do not let time make you forget your dua
outline.gist: The answer may come decades later, and the son granted reflected the patience Ibrahim showed.

outline.heading: Hajar and Ismail in the barren valley
outline.gist: Ibrahim left them where the Kaaba stood, a house that predates him and even Adam, saddened by how barren it was.

outline.heading: Zamzam and the Jurhum
outline.gist: The spring sustained Hajar, and a displaced Yemeni tribe asked her permission and paid to settle beside it; Ismail grew up and married among them.

outline.heading: All Ibrahim's descendants are Hebrews
outline.gist: Arabs through Ismail and Jews through Ishaq both descend from Ibrahim, so removing Palestinians to make room for 'the Hebrews' makes no sense.

outline.heading: When the son reached the age of working with him
outline.gist: The age when a son becomes helpful and a father is proudest of him.

outline.heading: The vision repeated three nights
outline.gist: Ibrahim hoped the first dream was from Shaytan; by the third night he knew it was revelation to slaughter his only, long-awaited son.

outline.heading: The great arguer does not argue
outline.gist: The Quran's example of critical thinking asks not one question here, because he knew this command was not debatable.

outline.heading: 'Do as you are commanded': both submit
outline.gist: Aslama means full submission of will; Ismail, raised to understand prophecy, tells his father he will be patient.

outline.heading: First be certain it is Allah's command

outline.heading: Shaytan at the jamarat

outline.heading: Face down, and the knife struck

outline.heading: You have fulfilled the vision: the clear trial

outline.heading: Ransomed because there was no benefit in it

outline.heading: Submission only when you understand is not submission

outline.heading: Ibrahim, the epitome of submission
outline.gist: He named us Muslims because he submitted his will without knowing the wisdom; Allah has no need for a child's blood.

outline.heading: Peace upon Ibrahim, and Ishaq fifty years later
outline.gist: His good name endures, and the good news of Ishaq came decades after, with both righteous and oppressive descendants.

k98vp0zBRRE.title: Ramadan Reminders 1446: Victory Is Not a Handout
k98vp0zBRRE.one_line: On the anniversary of the conquest of Mecca, as Gaza's bombing resumes: victory costs effort, unity and sacrifice, and dua alone is not enough.
k98vp0zBRRE.summary: Given on the 20th or 21st of Ramadan 1446, the anniversary of the conquest of Mecca and days after the bombing of Gaza resumed, this khutbah tries to make sense of an ummah weaker and more divided than at any point he can find in its history, watching children pulled from rubble in real time while the world looks away. Change, he insists, must begin deep inside each person and in how Muslims value one another, and the last ten nights are the time to start. The conquest is his model: it came after twenty-one years of effort through Badr, Uhud, the Trench, murdered teachers and the discipline of Hudaybiyyah, and the Prophet entered with his head bowed, turning Sa'd's day of slaughter into a day of mercy. Citing the Quran's repeated question of whether people expected Paradise without being tested, and Bani Israel's refusal to enter the Holy Land, he calls asking for victory while doing nothing, and while fighting over details, a lack of adab; less than one percent of Muslims are working, as he saw in Syria. Victory in Islam means people entering the faith in multitudes. If this generation is passed over, invest in the next. The second khutbah urges the Prophet's practice in the last ten nights and putting Allah's command before oneself.

outline.heading: Opening
Back on the minbar: an unprecedented weakness
outline.gist: Fifteen months on he must again make sense of events in the Holy Land. He knows the ummah's dark periods, but cannot find one with this degree of weakness, division and lack of voice; earlier ones had their own geopolitical and technological reasons.

outline.heading: Now we watch in real time
outline.gist: Past disasters struck distant states, and news arrived after it was over. Today we watch children pulled from rubble and people breathing their last on hospital floors with our own eyes.

outline.heading: A world that chooses to look away
outline.gist: The whole world sees it too and consciously turns a blind eye, whether from fear of the perpetrator or because the victims are valued so little. This cannot be our future; things must change.

outline.heading: Change begins deep inside
outline.gist: Change on a global scale must start in the depths of each person's consciousness and then in communities, until sixty thousand killed in a land smaller than London can no longer be justified.

outline.heading: If we do not value one another, no one will
outline.gist: Four hundred killed in a day while the world carries on trading cannot be acceptable. It begins with Muslims valuing, respecting and loving each other, and there is no better time than Ramadan's last ten nights.

outline.heading: The conquest of Mecca: returning differently
outline.gist: On the 20th or 21st of Ramadan, 8 AH, the Prophet returned to Mecca, no longer entering under conditions imposed on him but reclaiming it from those who held it by oppression.

outline.heading: Everyone wants the victory, few pay for it
outline.gist: We make dua for such a moment but will not put in the work. It does not come without tears, sweat and blood and millions devoting their lives to a cause bigger than themselves.

outline.heading: Entering Mecca with his head bowed
outline.gist: The conquest came after twenty-one years of lifelong effort. At sixty he entered with his face lowered to his camel's neck, overwhelmed by his Lord's generosity, the epitome of humility.

outline.heading: A day of mercy, not slaughter
outline.gist: When Sa'd ibn Ubadah declared it the day of slaughter, the Prophet took the banner from him, called it the day of mercy in which Quraysh would find its honour under Islam, and handed the banner to Sa'd's son.

outline.heading: Name the weakness before seeking solutions
outline.gist: Only when a two-billion-strong ummah spread over every continent admits how divided and weak it is can it begin talking about solutions.

outline.heading: Diversity without tokenism
outline.gist: Institutions manufacture diversity and put one face on a billboard. This masjid holds twenty-seven or twenty-eight nationalities effortlessly, the legacy of a Prophet who brought the message to all humanity.

outline.heading: Straight lines: no one stands ahead
outline.gist: Age, gender, wealth, status, culture and lineage make no difference in salah. No one may stand an inch ahead of the line, and no one may see himself as better.

outline.heading: What did you do with my ummah?
outline.gist: Real unity lives in the heart and puts the ummah's interest above your own agenda. Prepare an answer for when the Prophet asks what you did with the nation he left, rather than living in silos.

outline.heading: An annoying reminder: no going back to normal
outline.gist: Gaza keeps reminding us we cannot just enjoy quiet worship; just as we thought it had stopped, it resumed. The companions in Madinah also grew comfortable with the Prophet leading them in prayer.

outline.heading: From the caravan to the Trench
outline.gist: The Prophet told them there was much more work. The caravan sparked one struggle after another, Badr, Uhud and more, and before the conquest they shivered in cold and fear for days at the Trench.

outline.heading: Treachery, rumours and obedience
outline.gist: Muslims were betrayed, seventy teachers were murdered at Bi'r Ma'unah, and they faced social tests of rumours, military tests and a test of obedience when told to turn back at Hudaybiyyah.

outline.heading: Nothing comes for free
outline.gist: By the time you reach a goal the effort has shown its price. What comes too early is not valued, like wealth handed to the young; Allah grants the outcome after you put in the hours.

outline.heading: Did you think you would enter Paradise? (3:142)
outline.gist: Victory is not a handout. Allah asks again and again whether people expected Paradise, the ultimate triumph, before He exposed who would strive and persevere.

outline.heading: Shaken until they asked when help would come (2:214)
outline.gist: Earlier believers were shaken by psychological and religious earthquakes until even the Prophet among them asked when Allah's help would come. Help is near; the question is who will pay the price.

outline.heading: Dua alone is a lack of adab
outline.gist: Make dua for the people of Gaza, but if that is all, it misunderstands our role: Allah told us to care for the ummah, and we ask Him to do it for us. Musa told Bani Israel simply to enter the gate of Jerusalem.

outline.heading: Go, you and your Lord (5:21-24)
outline.gist: They replied that they would never go in: let Musa and his Lord fight and call them once it was won. We do the same when we raise our hands and do nothing, while actively dividing the ummah.

outline.heading: Less than one percent are working
outline.gist: We tear the ummah's fabric over tertiary details. Two billion people working at full strength could not produce this; less than one percent are working while the rest wait for different news on television.

outline.heading: Waiting for breaking news
outline.gist: He watched it in Syria: people did nothing but sat in front of Al Jazeera every Friday hoping to hear the regime had fallen. It took fifteen years, a million dead and countless drowned in the Mediterranean.

outline.heading: What victory means in Islam
outline.gist: It does not come cheap. Fath is not conquest but strength that draws people into Allah's religion in multitudes (110:2); our victory is people finding guidance.

outline.heading: Our weakness withholds guidance
outline.gist: Weakness lets children freeze barefoot and burn in their sleep, and it holds Allah's guidance back from others. Turn away and He will replace you with a people unlike you (47:38).

outline.heading: The forty years of wandering (5:26)
outline.gist: Allah lost hope in that generation and made them wander forty years until they died; not one of those who refused entered Jerusalem with Yusha'. He fears we are in that moment.

outline.heading: At least invest in the next generation
outline.gist: If Allah judges this generation not worth it and lets it live aimlessly, make sure you invest in the next one, so something comes after you.

outline.heading: Interlude
No more part-time commitment
outline.gist: No time of year is more blessed than the last ten nights. While asking Allah to change you inside, intend to change outside: His command and the Prophet's teaching first, your family next, yourself after. That is what submission means, and its fulfilment is found nowhere else.

outline.heading: Do what the Prophet did in the last ten nights
outline.gist: He let his family sleep through earlier Ramadan nights if they wished, but in the last ten he rolled up his sleeves, prayed most of the night and knocked on their doors to wake them.

outline.heading: The harder it is, the greater the reward
outline.gist: Tired, sleep-deprived and dehydrated, you gain more for the difficulty. He prays that Laylat al-Qadr becomes the beginning of change in the ummah.

outline.heading: Outro

JCh1gpy2pAE.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 18: Companionship
JCh1gpy2pAE.one_line: The Quran on companionship: the regret of one led astray by a friend, the people of the Fire with no intimate friend, and Sulayman's ant and hoopoe.
JCh1gpy2pAE.summary: He presents companionship as a universal truth: whatever you aim for, the people around you decide whether you get there. The Prophet called his followers companions rather than followers, and since time is the one capital that only decreases, you must be selective about who receives it, at every age and even more so as you get older and set in your ways. From 25:27-29 he describes the wrongdoer biting his hands in regret that can no longer be fixed, and tells the story of Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, who softened toward Islam while his best friend was away and then turned back at his friend's demand. He advises demoting harmful friends to a more distant circle rather than making them enemies. From 26:90-102 he draws that the people of the Fire have no intimate friend left outside to speak for them, that a bad friend acts as one of Iblis's soldiers, and that no one reaches Paradise or Hell alone. From 27:17-20 he reads the ant warning her community and Sulayman missing the hoopoe as signs that good companionship exists even among animals. He urges people to shed dead weight and attach their hearts to the right people, since a person is gathered with those he loves.

outline.heading: Companionship as a timeless concern
outline.gist: Every tradition stresses it because humans do not function without good company; bad company can ruin a life, and sometimes being alone is better than either.

outline.heading: Why the Prophet called them companions
outline.gist: He used 'ashab', not followers, signalling a group of friends working together and benefiting from each other rather than a leader with subordinates.

outline.heading: Time is the capital you can never recover
outline.gist: We are selective about money, holidays and clothes but should be most selective about who gets our hours.

outline.heading: Admitting a friendship was a waste
outline.gist: Looking back in your thirties or forties you may see friendships that gave nothing; be honest about whether the investment was worth it.

outline.heading: Companionship matters more as you age
outline.gist: Children change friends constantly, but older people grow set in their ways, so a poor circle is harder to escape; people in their forties and fifties whose friends are elsewhere feel foreign in the masjid.

outline.heading: Parents who drop their children at the masjid
outline.gist: Children learn by watching; he admires fathers who sit through lessons they do not need so that their children will.

outline.heading: You follow the religion of your best friend
outline.gist: You become like your closest friend; a like-minded friend who reminds you, lifts you and holds you accountable is a rare treasure.

outline.heading: The wrongdoer biting his hands
outline.gist: An Arabic expression for the deepest remorse, perhaps a form of punishing oneself.

outline.heading: Regret that can no longer be fixed
outline.gist: In this life you can still repent; on the Day of Judgment the outcome is fixed and regret peaks.

outline.heading: 'I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a friend'
outline.gist: The generic 'fulan' lets every reader apply it; the friend led him away from the reminder after it reached him.

outline.heading: Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt softens toward Islam
outline.gist: A fierce abuser of the Prophet began listening and stopped his harm while his best friend was away on a caravan.

outline.heading: His friend's ultimatum and the end at Badr
outline.gist: On returning, his friend refused to speak to him until he spat in the Prophet's face; he chose his friend and died beside him.

outline.heading: Shaytan always deserts you
outline.gist: The bad friend's influence feels like loyalty but pulls the heart away from Allah.

outline.heading: Circles of friendship: demote, do not make enemies
outline.gist: Move a harmful best friend to a more distant circle by being less available; explain if needed. This is an obligation, not an option.

outline.heading: Bad company cost him the Prophet's companionship
outline.gist: He could have been a sahabi but chose to be the companion of an enemy of the Prophet; choose who influences you before it is too late.

outline.heading: Paradise brought near; 'where are those you worshipped?'
outline.gist: Paradise is brought close to the mindful and Hell exposed to the lost, who are asked whether their false priorities can help them.

outline.heading: Thrown in together with the soldiers of Iblis
outline.gist: The doubled verb pictures them tipped in one after another, and the mention of Iblis's soldiers prepares what follows.

outline.heading: Quarrelling in the Fire
outline.gist: They admit they were lost when they equated others with the Lord of the worlds and blame the criminals who misled them.

outline.heading: No intercessor and no intimate friend
outline.gist: Everyone who cared about them is in the Fire with them; a single friend on the right side might have spoken for them.

outline.heading: A bad friend is a soldier of Iblis
outline.gist: We all know right from wrong; the bad friend makes the haram look normal and walks you several steps toward it.

outline.heading: Shaytan works through the person he has won
outline.gist: His whisper is weak and fades with a good deed, so he sends one fully indulging person into others' lives to infect them.

outline.heading: No one reaches Paradise or Hell alone
outline.gist: People are gathered in groups; except for a prophet whom no one followed, walking alone is not an option, and you go where your friends go.

outline.heading: Finding good friends is an obligation at any age
outline.gist: Without company that strengthens your iman you will not make it; distance yourself from those who do not help and find those who will.

outline.heading: Sulayman's army of jinn, men and birds
outline.gist: His sovereignty included soldiers of every kind gathered for him as they marched through a valley of ants.

outline.heading: The ant warns her community: why Sulayman smiled
outline.gist: He realised good companionship exists even among insects: someone who looks out for you and warns of danger.

outline.heading: Sulayman's gratitude for his companions
outline.gist: Danger is not always evil intent, yet you still need someone to warn you; Sulayman asks Allah to help him thank Him for the blessing of those around him.

outline.heading: 'Where is the hoopoe?' An animal as a better companion
outline.gist: The hoopoe's scouting brought Sulayman knowledge he could not have gained otherwise; some animals serve you better than some people.

outline.heading: Shed the dead weight
outline.gist: Here you must put yourself first: help those you can, but when someone only takes you away from Allah, remove them sooner rather than later.

outline.heading: Gathered with those your heart loved
outline.gist: On the Day of Judgment a person is with the people he loved, so attach your heart to the right group now, especially before age sets you in your ways.

themes.label: Brotherhood, companionship and friendship
themes.note: Companions shape who you become in this life and whom you stand with in the next; choose them, demote harmful ones and shed dead weight.

themes.label: Time, opportunity and seizing the moment
themes.note: Time is the only capital that always decreases, so whom you spend it with is a major decision.

themes.label: The masjid: its role and etiquette
themes.note: Older people whose friends are elsewhere struggle to enter the masjid, and parents must attend with their children rather than drop them off.

themes.label: Seerah events and their lessons
themes.note: Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt lost the chance to be a companion of the Prophet because of his best friend.

themes.label: The Hereafter: resurrection, judgment, paradise, hellfire
themes.note: Final regret, the people of the Fire without an intimate friend, and being gathered in groups with those you kept company with.

themes.label: Shaytan: his methods and how to resist him
themes.note: Shaytan's whisper is weak; his real tool is a person he has won over, sent into others' lives as a bad friend.

18:9.ar: أَمۡ حَسِبۡتَ أَنَّ أَصۡحَٰبَ ٱلۡكَهۡفِ وَٱلرَّقِيمِ كَانُواْ مِنۡ ءَايَٰتِنَا عَجَبًا
18:9.en: Or have you thought that the companions of the cave and the inscription were, among Our signs, a wonder

10:90.ar: ۞وَجَٰوَزۡنَا بِبَنِيٓ إِسۡرَٰٓءِيلَ ٱلۡبَحۡرَ فَأَتۡبَعَهُمۡ فِرۡعَوۡنُ وَجُنُودُهُۥ بَغۡيࣰ ا وَعَدۡوًاۖ حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَآ أَدۡرَكَهُ ٱلۡغَرَقُ قَالَ ءَامَنتُ أَنَّهُۥ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا ٱلَّذِيٓ ءَامَنَتۡ بِهِۦ بَنُوٓاْ إِسۡرَٰٓءِيلَ وَأَنَا۠ مِنَ ٱلۡمُسۡلِمِينَ
10:90.en: And We took the Children of Israel across the sea, and Pharaoh and his soldiers pursued them in tyranny and enmity until, when drowning overtook him, he said, "I believe that there is no deity except that in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims

10:91.ar: ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ وَقَدۡ عَصَيۡتَ قَبۡلُ وَكُنتَ مِنَ ٱلۡمُفۡسِدِينَ
10:91.en: Now? And you had disobeyed [Him] before and were of the corrupters

4:135.ar: ۞يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ كُونُواْ قَوَّٰمِينَ بِٱلۡقِسۡطِ شُهَدَآءَ لِلَّهِ وَلَوۡ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِكُمۡ أَوِ ٱلۡوَٰلِدَيۡنِ وَٱلۡأَقۡرَبِينَۚ إِن يَكُنۡ غَنِيًّا أَوۡ فَقِيرࣰ ا فَٱللَّهُ أَوۡلَىٰ بِهِمَاۖ فَلَا تَتَّبِعُواْ ٱلۡهَوَىٰٓ أَن تَعۡدِلُواْۚ وَإِن تَلۡوُۥٓاْ أَوۡ تُعۡرِضُواْ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ خَبِيرࣰ ا
4:135.en: O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives. Whether one is rich or poor, Allah is more worthy of both. So follow not [personal] inclination, lest you not be just. And if you distort [your testimony] or refuse [to give it], then indeed Allah is ever, with what you do, Acquainted

18:17.ar: ۞وَتَرَى ٱلشَّمۡسَ إِذَا طَلَعَت تَّزَٰوَرُ عَن كَهۡفِهِمۡ ذَاتَ ٱلۡيَمِينِ وَإِذَا غَرَبَت تَّقۡرِضُهُمۡ ذَاتَ ٱلشِّمَالِ وَهُمۡ فِي فَجۡوَةࣲ مِّنۡهُۚ ذَٰلِكَ مِنۡ ءَايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِۗ مَن يَهۡدِ ٱللَّهُ فَهُوَ ٱلۡمُهۡتَدِۖ وَمَن يُضۡلِلۡ فَلَن تَجِدَ لَهُۥ وَلِيࣰّ ا مُّرۡشِدࣰ ا
18:17.en: And [had you been present], you would see the sun when it rose, inclining away from their cave on the right, and when it set, passing away from them on the left, while they were [laying] within an open space thereof. That was from the signs of Allah. He whom Allah guides is the [rightly] guided, but he whom He leaves astray - never will you find for him a protecting guide

18:14.ar: وَرَبَطۡنَا عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمۡ إِذۡ قَامُواْ فَقَالُواْ رَبُّنَا رَبُّ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ لَن نَّدۡعُوَاْ مِن دُونِهِۦٓ إِلَٰهࣰ اۖ لَّقَدۡ قُلۡنَآ إِذࣰ ا شَطَطًا
18:14.en: And We made firm their hearts when they stood up and said, "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. Never will we invoke besides Him any deity. We would have certainly spoken, then, an excessive transgression

18:13.ar: نَّحۡنُ نَقُصُّ عَلَيۡكَ نَبَأَهُم بِٱلۡحَقِّۚ إِنَّهُمۡ فِتۡيَةٌ ءَامَنُواْ بِرَبِّهِمۡ وَزِدۡنَٰهُمۡ هُدࣰ ى
18:13.en: It is We who relate to you, [O Muhammad], their story in truth. Indeed, they were youths who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance

18:19.ar: وَكَذَٰلِكَ بَعَثۡنَٰهُمۡ لِيَتَسَآءَلُواْ بَيۡنَهُمۡۚ قَالَ قَآئِلࣱ مِّنۡهُمۡ كَمۡ لَبِثۡتُمۡۖ قَالُواْ لَبِثۡنَا يَوۡمًا أَوۡ بَعۡضَ يَوۡمࣲۚ قَالُواْ رَبُّكُمۡ أَعۡلَمُ بِمَا لَبِثۡتُمۡ فَٱبۡعَثُوٓاْ أَحَدَكُم بِوَرِقِكُمۡ هَٰذِهِۦٓ إِلَى ٱلۡمَدِينَةِ فَلۡيَنظُرۡ أَيُّهَآ أَزۡكَىٰ طَعَامࣰ ا فَلۡيَأۡتِكُم بِرِزۡقࣲ مِّنۡهُ وَلۡيَتَلَطَّفۡ وَلَا يُشۡعِرَنَّ بِكُمۡ أَحَدًا
18:19.en: And similarly, We awakened them that they might question one another. Said a speaker from among them, "How long have you remained [here]?" They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day." They said, "Your Lord is most knowing of how long you remained. So send one of you with this silver coin of yours to the city and let him look to which is the best of food and bring you provision from it and let him be cautious. And let no one be aware of you

9:24.ar: قُلۡ إِن كَانَ ءَابَآؤُكُمۡ وَأَبۡنَآؤُكُمۡ وَإِخۡوَٰنُكُمۡ وَأَزۡوَٰجُكُمۡ وَعَشِيرَتُكُمۡ وَأَمۡوَٰلٌ ٱقۡتَرَفۡتُمُوهَا وَتِجَٰرَةࣱ تَخۡشَوۡنَ كَسَادَهَا وَمَسَٰكِنُ تَرۡضَوۡنَهَآ أَحَبَّ إِلَيۡكُم مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦ وَجِهَادࣲ فِي سَبِيلِهِۦ فَتَرَبَّصُواْ حَتَّىٰ يَأۡتِيَ ٱللَّهُ بِأَمۡرِهِۦۗ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يَهۡدِي ٱلۡقَوۡمَ ٱلۡفَٰسِقِينَ
9:24.en: Say, [O Muhammad], "If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your wives, your relatives, wealth which you have obtained, commerce wherein you fear decline, and dwellings with which you are pleased are more beloved to you than Allah and His Messenger and jihad in His cause, then wait until Allah executes His command. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people

9:111.ar: ۞إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ ٱشۡتَرَىٰ مِنَ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ أَنفُسَهُمۡ وَأَمۡوَٰلَهُم بِأَنَّ لَهُمُ ٱلۡجَنَّةَۚ يُقَٰتِلُونَ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ فَيَقۡتُلُونَ وَيُقۡتَلُونَۖ وَعۡدًا عَلَيۡهِ حَقࣰّ ا فِي ٱلتَّوۡرَىٰةِ وَٱلۡإِنجِيلِ وَٱلۡقُرۡءَانِۚ وَمَنۡ أَوۡفَىٰ بِعَهۡدِهِۦ مِنَ ٱللَّهِۚ فَٱسۡتَبۡشِرُواْ بِبَيۡعِكُمُ ٱلَّذِي بَايَعۡتُم بِهِۦۚ وَذَٰلِكَ هُوَ ٱلۡفَوۡزُ ٱلۡعَظِيمُ
9:111.en: Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties [in exchange] for that they will have Paradise. They fight in the cause of Allah, so they kill and are killed. [It is] a true promise [binding] upon Him in the Torah and the Gospel and the Qur'an. And who is truer to his covenant than Allah? So rejoice in your transaction which you have contracted. And it is that which is the great attainment

L2rA6xxgdho.title: Pointing Out the Obvious 1: Qiyam (Taking a Stand)
L2rA6xxgdho.one_line: First of seven sessions: for the companions it was obvious that Islam meant total commitment to a cause, taking a stand and proving it.
L2rA6xxgdho.summary: The series argues that much of what we reach only after years of study was simply obvious to the companions, because every civilization drifts from the values that built it. This first session takes qiyam, which means taking a stand rather than standing up. He gives four senses: activism as prioritizing a cause, establishing a position that your deeds will reveal whether you state it or not, dedication and commitment, and the willingness to sacrifice comfort, sleep and leisure. Saying you stand for something is cheap until you prove it. Standing for justice may mean testifying against yourself and your parents, as An-Nisa demands. The people of the cave show what a few youths who took a stand can achieve: their kingdom changed after three hundred years, and Allah woke them to show them their stand mattered. He pictures the Prophet's ordered stack of priorities scattered over centuries, leaving people agitated over tertiary questions. Fear of discovering one's mediocrity, resistance and unresolved doubts hold people back. Partial commitment brings no personal benefit, weakens communities, misrepresents Islam and leaves room for extremists. He asks each listener to find the area of service their own life experiences have prepared them for.

outline.heading: Opening
What was obvious to the companions
outline.gist: Concepts we reach after years of study were the norm for the Prophet and his companions; they would wonder why anyone needed a series to point them out.

outline.heading: Every civilization drifts from its founding values
outline.gist: Western civilization was built on freedom from tyranny, which mutated into the right to own a gun, offend God openly and walk around naked.

outline.heading: A renewer every hundred years
outline.gist: Allah sends people to reset the ummah's mindset each century; it has been some eighty-five years since the last, so we must refocus on the simple, profound core of the deen.

outline.heading: Qiyam means taking a stand, not posture
outline.gist: The word was iconic for the companions' generation; its figurative sense, taking a stand, is the real one.

outline.heading: Obviously we commit one hundred percent
outline.gist: The paragraph that opens each session: we are expected to commit fully to Allah's teachings, advocate for His cause and dedicate life and wealth to Him.

outline.heading: No one entered Islam the way we live it
outline.gist: The shahada came with offering everything; no one gave the Prophet allegiance and then lived as we do today.

outline.heading: Command us regarding our lives
outline.gist: Apart from one group he declines to name, everyone came asking what to do with their lives, wealth and families, which is why Islam did not fade after the Prophet's death.

outline.heading: Islam spread to three continents in fifty years
outline.gist: Christianity struggled for centuries until a ruler adopted it and blended in pagan culture, while Islam became the largest and most diverse empire within fifty years of the Prophet's death.

outline.heading: Not a part-time membership
outline.gist: Giving Islam only your spare time and wealth means other priorities come first, which the companions never understood as acceptable.

outline.heading: First meaning: activism, prioritizing a cause
outline.gist: An activist simply prioritizes a cause, like environmentalists who can be annoying to those who do not share it. What does a Muslim prioritize?

outline.heading: People commit to causes that serve humanity
outline.gist: The companions knew from their shahada that the deen, a system for people to live well, came first. Activism is for causes beyond oneself; advocating for one person is different.

outline.heading: Islam balances personal interest
outline.gist: Islam wants you to have ambition, provide for your family and enjoy life, but none of that is placed above the cause you live for.

outline.heading: Second meaning: establishing a position
outline.gist: All that remains after death is what you stood for. You will stand for something, just as no one can avoid having a religion; even indifference to life's questions is one.

outline.heading: Your deeds will articulate your stand
outline.gist: If you will not state it, it will be read from the story you wrote. Stating it reminds you and gathers like-minded companions, because standing alone is crippling.

outline.heading: The poet and the king
outline.gist: A poet heaped exaggerated praise on a king who kept naming larger rewards; the king told his steward that words were paid with words. A stand must be proven with action.

outline.heading: Third meaning: dedication and commitment
outline.gist: Today people will not even say that Islam comes before their personal and family interests, let alone prove it, which is a lifelong struggle.

outline.heading: The biggest obstacle is commitment
outline.gist: Asked at an early town hall what his biggest obstacle was, he answered commitment. Most people float in and out of masjid work for a few years.

outline.heading: Imagine Abu Bakr taking a year off
outline.gist: Picture Umar on vacation or a companion pausing for a career; those who did so are not even named in history.

outline.heading: Even Abu Jahl stuck to his stand
outline.gist: People who commit to a cause are remembered even when it is wrong. Pharaoh's last-minute belief was rejected.

outline.heading: Fourth meaning: willingness to sacrifice
outline.gist: Sacrifice is giving up leisure, sleep, wealth, luxury and status you could otherwise have, because something more important is at hand.

outline.heading: A society organized around vacations
outline.gist: Hospital colleagues talk mostly about their last and next trip; Muslims living among them adopt the same priority.

outline.heading: Allah tests your stated priorities
outline.gist: If Islam fills only spare room, Allah brings a conflict that forces a choice, and the choice reveals your real stand. He keeps giving chances, but you never know the last one.

outline.heading: Standing firm for justice, even against yourself
outline.gist: An-Nisa commands believers to stand for justice as witnesses for Allah even against themselves, their parents and relatives.

outline.heading: Would you testify against your mother?
outline.gist: Few in his sessions say yes, because their priorities are wrong. You love and honour your mother, but justice comes before everyone.

outline.heading: Help your brother by restraining him
outline.gist: Activism for family leads to defending relatives in their wrongs; the Prophet taught that helping a wrongdoing brother means stopping him. Something must stand above spouse, children and self.

outline.heading: The village of the people of the cave
outline.gist: A small village near Amman is believed to be where the cave dwellers sought refuge; it reminds him of the village he came from.

outline.heading: The story we recite every Friday
outline.gist: Al-Kahf is the only surah set for weekly recitation, and its first pages carry this story, so even those who never finish reach it.

outline.heading: Or did you think it was a one-time wonder?
outline.gist: The surah opens as if mid-conversation: did you think the cave was a freak event? Allah bent the laws of nature for them to teach that He does this again for people like them.

outline.heading: They stood up: refusing the status quo
outline.gist: Their qiyam was taking a stand when they would no longer sit on the sidelines while their nation was misled and corrupted.

outline.heading: Fityah: youths without experience
outline.gist: The word describes people under twenty with little life behind them, perhaps only three, yet they put something above themselves.

outline.heading: A stand without abandoning family
outline.gist: Prioritizing the cause does not mean neglecting wife, children or family; it means having the list in the right order.

outline.heading: The scattered stack of priorities
outline.gist: The Prophet stacked life's elements in perfect order and generations carried it, until someone dropped it and restacked it wrongly without telling anyone; the damage shows only centuries later.

outline.heading: Fighting over tertiary issues
outline.gist: Until the stack is restored, people will stay agitated over matters scholars have differed on for centuries, like the yearly moonsighting debate and facial hair.

outline.heading: Your job is the stand, not the outcome
outline.gist: The obvious point is that accepting Allah dedicates your life to something; Allah showed the youths that results are His concern.

outline.heading: Why did they wake up?
outline.gist: Their written creed was found and taught for generations until the king fell. Allah woke them, though they died soon after, to show them their stand made a difference.

outline.heading: The coin with his own face on it
outline.gist: He imagines the youth sent to buy food finding his old silver worthless and his own face on the currency and a statue of the group, then returning to learn the corruption had ended.

outline.heading: The Quran assumes full commitment
outline.gist: The Quran repeats striving with wealth and lives as a given rather than explaining it, because the purpose of life is serving Allah.

outline.heading: The upright religion and the Prophet's example
outline.gist: The religion called qayyim, from the same root, gives you a stand: straight with a purpose, never reordering priorities for personal gain. The Prophet is its ultimate example.

outline.heading: Eight loves and the sale of lives
outline.gist: In At-Tawbah Allah lists eight things we may love and warns those who love them more than Him, His Prophet and striving; He has bought the believers' lives and wealth for Paradise.

outline.heading: Tawbah from a lifestyle
outline.gist: The surah, revealed about those who stayed behind from Tabuk, is about repenting from a way of life in which Allah and His deen are not first.

outline.heading: Where would the Prophet be? Go there
outline.gist: Those questions are easy to answer. The early Muslims stood against paganism, corruption and racism, which made the deen attractive.

outline.heading: After Hudaybiyyah the numbers soared
outline.gist: Once the treaty let people see Islam, numbers multiplied within a year, because people long to live for something bigger than themselves and Paradise waits beyond it.

outline.heading: Indifference and performative activism
outline.gist: Plato: the price of indifference is being ruled by evil men. Performative activism enjoys the reputation of a cause without the work.

outline.heading: Performative activism in the deen
outline.gist: Claiming to stand for Islam without the time and commitment to show it. He praises sociology as an underrated science that helps Muslims understand their own texts.

outline.heading: Full commitment lightens the mind
outline.gist: Research shows that committing fully to a goal reduces cognitive load and simplifies decisions: you know A comes first and do not regret B.

outline.heading: Hindrance one: fear of finding out you are mediocre
outline.gist: Vanity makes us hold back so that a mediocre result never measures our full effort.

outline.heading: We are all mediocre
outline.gist: Only one in ten million has Messi's natural gift; everyone else gets good through hard work. After twenty-five years of public speaking he still calls himself mediocre: acknowledge it, learn and improve.

outline.heading: Commit even if you barely move the needle
outline.gist: We only want to commit if we will be the hero; you may give everything and be remembered by ten people, and that is fine.

outline.heading: Hindrance two: resistance from people
outline.gist: Taking a stand brings pushback. He keeps away from people who want to be on everyone's side; tell him what you stand for and common ground can be found. That takes courage.

outline.heading: Hindrance three: cognitive dissonance
outline.gist: Unaddressed doubts and a belief system out of line with reality make commitment hard; deal with them by seeking knowledge.

outline.heading: Individual commitment to a group effort
outline.gist: Islam is bigger than any masjid or country; when enough individuals channel their effort relentlessly in one direction, social norms shift.

outline.heading: Consequence one: Islam will not work for you
outline.gist: Taken part-time, Islam gives no benefit and you will wonder why you feel nothing; give the Quran everything to receive a little that lasts.

outline.heading: All in or all out
outline.gist: Islam does not reward ninety percent. He does not judge anyone's level, but the half-committed get neither the believer's reward nor the life they wanted, which is why the Quran dwells on hypocrisy.

outline.heading: Consequence two: communities fail
outline.gist: Too much dead weight takes services and walks away. Medina built no castles; its companions dispersed after the Prophet's death and taught the world.

outline.heading: Consequence three: false representation
outline.gist: Partial commitment gives children, peers and non-Muslims the wrong idea of Islam, a sin we will carry.

outline.heading: Consequence four: making room for extremism
outline.gist: Good people stand outside criticizing those at the front of the masjid; when they do not step in, the misguided take centre stage, and the rest of us share the blame.

outline.heading: A committed community leaves no room for extremism
outline.gist: Where every role is filled by someone educated and doing the work properly, fundamentalist narratives find no space.

outline.heading: Find your compartment in the deen
outline.gist: Commitment does not mean doing everything. Your space will grow from your life story: a broken family or a troubled youth points to the problem you will work on.

outline.heading: Your experiences are opportunities
outline.gist: Some find their place in philanthropy, dawah, counselling or youth work. Allah gives hard experiences as openings, just as the best addiction counsellors are former addicts.

JdTV60lyipo.title: Zakat 101: How to Calculate Your Zakat
JdTV60lyipo.one_line: A practical guide to who owes zakat and how to calculate it on cash, jewelry, businesses, stocks, registered accounts, property and debts, and where to give it.
JdTV60lyipo.summary: The presenter frames zakat as both a purification of wealth that is never fully free of haram and a share of one's money that no longer belongs to the owner, warning that many careful Muslims fall years behind without realizing they are holding what is not theirs. Zakat is owed by a free, adult Muslim who holds the nisab, roughly the silver standard, for a full lunar year; it falls on saved wealth, not on income. He walks through each asset type: cash tallied on one fixed lunar date, gold and silver at current value, business cash, inventory and receivables minus current liabilities, and stocks, where he recommends paying on the company's short-term assets rather than market value. He argues that RRSPs, TFSAs and similar accounts should be zakated in full, since the owner invests the deferred tax as his own, while pensions and unvested shares are not owned yet. Personal-use property is exempt, rental income counts only once saved, and only debts due that year are deducted. He closes with the eight recipient categories, giving locally through reputable charities, common mistakes such as using a solar date or delaying, and how zakat pushes idle cash into productive investment.

outline.heading: Opening
What zakat purifies
outline.gist: Zakat cleanses wealth of the unintentional haram that always mixes in, and marks a share that no longer belongs to the owner; keeping it is like consuming haram, yet people strict about halal meat fall years behind on zakat.

outline.heading: Who owes zakat: nisab and the lunar year
outline.gist: A free, adult Muslim whose savings reach the nisab for a full lunar year pays; the simple test is whether you are someone who would receive zakat. Scholars favour the lower silver standard, and a solar year falls behind by a full year every three decades.

outline.heading: Zakat is on saved wealth, not income
outline.gist: Unlike Canadian income tax, zakat ignores earnings and falls on what is saved for a year. He argues the Islamic system is better for the economy, but people prefer short-term gain over long-term benefit.

outline.heading: Which cash has completed a year; the 2.5 percent rate
outline.gist: Strictly, each deposit has its own year, which forces several payments. The rate of one quarter of a tenth comes from the Prophet, not the Quran, which shows why the sunnah is indispensable.

outline.heading: Pick one lunar date and tally every account
outline.gist: Choose a date, ideally in Ramadan, add all accounts and currencies including cash held for travel, and pay 2.5 percent; early and late deposits even out over the years.

outline.heading: Gold and silver jewelry
outline.gist: Treated like currency at 2.5 percent of current value. The Shafi'i school exempts jewelry worn for adornment, while the Hanafi school includes it because it can be sold.

outline.heading: Business assets
outline.gist: Productive capital such as equipment and buildings is not zakatable; a business pays on cash, inventory and receivables minus current liabilities.

outline.heading: Stocks: market value or treated as farmland
outline.gist: Paying on full market value suits day traders but not long-term holders. Some scholars treat shares like farmland, paying 5 or 10 percent of the dividend harvest, which he finds a poor analogy.

outline.heading: Stocks: zakat on the company's short-term assets
outline.gist: His recommended method splits a company into long-term capital, exempt, and short-term assets, zakated at 2.5 percent; once dismissed, it is now used by most zakat calculators.

outline.heading: RRSPs, TFSAs and corporate accounts
outline.gist: Some exclude the future tax share, but he argues the owner invests that share as his own, the future rate is unknown and no one else will zakat it, so pay on the full amount and be generous with Allah, since charity never decreases wealth.

outline.heading: Pensions and unvested shares
outline.gist: CPP, employer pensions and unvested stock are not owned until received or vested, so no zakat is due on them until then.

outline.heading: Personal-use property is exempt
outline.gist: Homes, cars, watches and cottages kept for personal use carry no zakat, however many there are.

outline.heading: Interlude
Rental property
outline.gist: The property itself is not zakatable; only rental income that remains saved after a year is.

outline.heading: Deducting debts you owe
outline.gist: Subtract only what falls due within the zakat year; a mortgage or long loan does not excuse decades of zakat.

outline.heading: Money owed to you
outline.gist: A lender pays zakat on a loan he expects to recover; if he has given up on it, none is due until it becomes collectible again, and then only for that year.

outline.heading: The eight categories of recipients
outline.gist: Zakat may only go to the categories Allah names, so tell a charity the money is zakat; otherwise it can be used for general expenses.

outline.heading: Giving locally
outline.gist: Zakat is meant to return to the community where it was earned; some may go to disasters abroad, but neglecting local need is a problem, which is why a community funds network was set up.

outline.heading: Choosing a charity
outline.gist: Charities give tax receipts and donating securities can be very effective. Check reputation and admin ratios, but an admin cost near zero is a warning sign of underinvestment.

outline.heading: Common mistakes
outline.gist: Using a fixed solar date, lending money out to dodge zakat, assuming a mortgage exempts you, miscalculating investments, and delaying payment once it is due; paying early is fine.

outline.heading: The philosophy of zakat
outline.gist: Zakat penalizes idle cash and interest-based lending is barred, so wealth flows into investment; if Muslims did this properly the economy would flourish, since Allah wants believers strong and wealthy in the right way.

outline.heading: Outro

B_pjdVrMBUw.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 15: Taqwa and Jihad
B_pjdVrMBUw.one_line: Taqwa as a preventive safety valve against future pain and jihad as a mindset of lifelong striving, completing a practical toolkit with tawakkul.
B_pjdVrMBUw.summary: He argues that Muslims overlook simple fundamentals while chasing details, and presents two of them. Taqwa linguistically means prevention: guarding yourself before harm happens, which is incomparably better than repenting after, since crossing a red line once makes crossing it again far more likely. Pain is not all bad; some is necessary for growth, but the pain worth preventing is the useless kind, ultimately Hellfire. Taqwa works as a safety valve: before any decision ask whether it will harm you or bring regret later, a simpler test than asking whether it pleases Allah, and one that respects Allah's warnings and demands foresight reaching beyond death. He draws a parallel with preventive medicine, which is underfunded because it does not pay. Jihad is a mentality of striving against the self, sin, difficulty and oppression, entering life expecting obstacles rather than cruise control. If your whole life is striving for Allah, everything that sustains it, even leisure and marital intimacy, becomes worship, just as a company covers the costs of a business trip. Taqwa, tawakkul and jihad together form a practical toolkit. Tazkiyah means pushing back when the self resists asking the taqwa question or feels entitled to ease for being good. These simple concepts transformed the companions, and they rest on the foundations covered earlier in the series.

outline.heading: Overlooked fundamentals
outline.gist: We get preoccupied with details while simple core teachings go unpractised or mispractised.

outline.heading: Taqwa: the goal of every act of worship
outline.gist: Mentioned some 258 times in the Quran, taqwa is the clothing, nourishment and foundation of a Muslim's life.

outline.heading: Taqwa means prevention
outline.gist: From the root of protecting yourselves and your families, it is a preventive attitude; preventing sin is far better than repenting after.

outline.heading: Once a line is crossed, it is easier to cross again
outline.gist: When nothing happens after a first transgression the self relaxes; studies of reoffending show repeat breaches are far more likely.

outline.heading: Not all pain is bad
outline.gist: Feeling pain marks life itself, and some pain is needed for growth.

outline.heading: The useless pain taqwa prevents
outline.gist: Hellfire is the ultimate unnecessary pain, but neglecting health also brings pointless suffering; the self and soul both fear pain.

outline.heading: The safety valve: will this harm me later?
outline.gist: Ask one question before any decision; if the answer is yes, do not do it.

outline.heading: Taqwa versus the higher question of pleasing Allah
outline.gist: Asking whether something pleases Allah belongs to love and narrows choices; taqwa leaves open everything good or permissible.

outline.heading: Taqwa as respect for Allah's warning
outline.gist: Not guarding against what Allah warned of shows you do not take the warning seriously, a failure of adab.

outline.heading: Taqwa requires foresight beyond death
outline.gist: A Muslim connects present decisions to the near and far future, as far as after death.

outline.heading: Preventive medicine and the real pharma failure
outline.gist: The problem is not a hidden cancer cure but that prevention and screening go unfunded because they do not pay; communities must fund them.

outline.heading: Jihad as a way of life
outline.gist: Striving against the self, sin, difficulty, disbelief and oppression, and towards hard good deeds.

outline.heading: Expect obstacles, not cruise control
outline.gist: Life is designed as trial for everyone; expecting struggle keeps your guard up and your energy ready.

JfRfr6X77Mg.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 16: Quranic Themes, Your Relationship with Allah
JfRfr6X77Mg.one_line: The unique relationship with Allah: dhikr that brings contentment (20:130), Yunus owning his mistake in the whale (21:87-88), and reverence for Allah's rituals (22:32).
JfRfr6X77Mg.summary: He separates three Quranic themes: knowing Allah, which grounds faith; obeying Allah, which rests on the difference in status between Creator and creation; and the relationship with Allah, a lifelong path with no limit to how close one can come, and the true theme of Ramadan. No other relationship resembles it, since Allah is unseen and does not reply in words, and we struggle even with human relationships. Yet research such as the long Harvard study shows relationships are what bring people fulfilment, and this one brings the most; in Ramadan Allah opens the door for a fresh start. From 20:130 he explains that the Prophet, whose plan to win Makkah did not unfold as hoped, was told to persevere and glorify his Lord at every hour so that he would be content: dhikr gains Allah nothing and gives us everything. From 21:87-88 he retells Yunus leaving his people in anger without permission, the three lots, and his words in the whale's belly, an apology that fully owns the mistake, which Allah promises to answer for every believer in their own darkness. From 22:32 he teaches that revering Allah's rituals and commands is the sign of taqwa in the heart.

outline.heading: Knowing, obeying and relating to Allah
outline.gist: Knowing Allah comes before belief; obedience rests on the gap between the finite servant and the infinite Lord; the relationship is a third, separate theme.

outline.heading: A top Quranic theme
outline.gist: Whole passages and surahs describe what to aim for, avoid and repair in the relationship with Allah.

outline.heading: A lifelong path and the theme of Ramadan
outline.gist: There is no end to how close or how far one can be, and mending this relationship is what Ramadan is for.

outline.heading: No other relationship is like it
outline.gist: He is unseen and does not answer in words; we barely manage relationships we practise daily, so this one needs sensitivity to how He responds.

outline.heading: The most beautiful relationship of all
outline.gist: Parents, spouse, children and friends bring deep fulfilment, but this relationship, built well, surpasses them.

outline.heading: What brings people happiness
outline.gist: A 75-year Harvard study found that beyond basic needs, meaningful relationships, not money or fame, gave people satisfaction and longer lives.

outline.heading: Ramadan's open door
outline.gist: The most fulfilling relationship is with Allah, who in Ramadan offers a new page as if you had never sinned, because He created you for this.

outline.heading: The finite connecting with the Infinite
outline.gist: A mortal finding connection with the Divine, beyond time and space, is what makes life worthwhile, and ignoring it is a tragedy.

outline.heading: Be patient with what they say
outline.gist: Facing rejection and mockery, the Prophet was told to persevere, since guidance cannot be forced on those you love.

outline.heading: Plans that did not work out
outline.gist: He planned to win Quraysh's leaders, then Makkah, then the Arabs, and it did not happen; plans rarely go as hoped, so adapt.

outline.heading: Glorify your Lord at every hour
outline.gist: Before sunrise, before sunset, in the night and at the ends of the day: engage in praise at every moment you find.

outline.heading: So that you may be content
outline.gist: Praising Allah adds nothing to Him; the result is a calm and satisfaction you could not find any other way.

outline.heading: All the benefit is ours
outline.gist: The relationship is built on what is in it for us: contentment instead of always chasing the next thing, which is why we come every night.

outline.heading: Dhun-Nun storms out in anger
outline.gist: Yunus was angry at his people, not at Allah, for refusing to listen after three days' warning, and left the city.

outline.heading: A prophet may not leave without permission
outline.gist: He thought he would not be held to account because he acted out of love, and he was wrong.

outline.heading: His people were destined to repent
outline.gist: Within those three days his people were to repent and be forgiven, and by leaving he left them no one to turn to.

outline.heading: Three straws
outline.gist: On an overloaded ship they drew lots to throw someone overboard, and his name came up three times, so he understood the message.

outline.heading: A noble feeling, a wrong assessment
outline.gist: His grief for his people looks noble, but Allah's terms with His prophets are clear; he went overboard and was swallowed.

outline.heading: Ashamed in the belly of the whale
outline.gist: Distressed and ashamed, he had the self-accountability to admit the decision was never his to make, and saw his plight as mercy.

outline.heading: Searching for the right words
outline.gist: Apology or a plea for forgiveness seemed too little to express his remorse.

outline.heading: There is no god but You
outline.gist: His words declare Allah's oneness and perfection and confess wrongdoing; the Prophet said any servant who says them in hardship is given ease.

outline.heading: Darkness upon darkness
outline.gist: It is an apology without detail: You are right and I was wrong; in the darkness of the whale, the sea and the night, the words were his light.

outline.heading: Everyone has a belly of the whale
outline.gist: Allah saved him and promises to save believers likewise; we all face isolation and shame, and calling on Him with these words begins the way out.

outline.heading: Owning the mistake
outline.gist: In an unforeseeable situation he blamed no one but himself; turn to Allah in your darkness with that same remorse.

outline.heading: Magnifying the rituals of Allah
outline.gist: Reverence is the basis of the relationship: we use fitting titles for the Prophet, parents and teachers, and the companions would not stare at his face.

outline.heading: A sign of taqwa in the heart
outline.gist: How much you revere Allah's commands and rituals shows whether your heart has taqwa; praise for contentment, repentance in despair, and reverence form the relationship.

outline.heading: Outro

93Ma0f6bKDs.title: Ramadan 2025, Night 21: First Night of Tahajjud
93Ma0f6bKDs.one_line: Opening a series on the movements of the prayer: the standing as a dialogue with Allah, the Prophet's long recitation, and bowing.
93Ma0f6bKDs.summary: On the twenty-first night of Ramadan 2025 the sheikh begins a series for the last ten nights on the movements of the prayer. We do not pray in a single posture, he says, because each movement is meant to do something different to the soul. In the first reminder he takes the standing. It is the longest part of the best prayer, and in it we recite Allah's words back to Him, memorized word for word, with reflection and love. He explains the hadith qudsi in which Allah answers each verse of Al-Fatiha, tells how Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz paused after every verse to imagine his Lord's reply, and teaches that Allah faces the worshipper for as long as the worshipper faces Him, turning away once something else matters more in the heart. In the second reminder he shows how the Prophet and his companions found joy in the standing: Ibn Mas'ud's recitation of An-Nisa that brought the Prophet to tears, and the night prayer in which the Prophet recited Al-Baqarah, An-Nisa and Aal-Imran in one rakah, pausing to ask for Paradise and refuge from the Fire. He then turns to bowing, which once meant taking a knee before someone greater, and to the words of glorification and surrender said in it.

outline.heading: Interlude
These nights are for the prayer itself
outline.gist: He sets the prayer itself as the subject of his reminders on these nights, since nothing is more worth talking about while standing in it.

outline.heading: Each movement mirrors a change in the spirit
outline.gist: We do not pray in one posture; we stand, bow, rise, prostrate and sit because each movement is meant to do something different inside us, bringing humility and clarity.

outline.heading: Standing: reciting His words back to Him
outline.gist: The best prayer is the one with the longest standing; in it we show that we have not only accepted and applied His revelation but memorized it word for word and recite it back to Him with reflection and love.

outline.heading: Allah answers each verse of Al-Fatiha
outline.gist: In the hadith qudsi Allah divides the prayer between Himself and His servant: He replies 'My servant has praised Me', 'has glorified Me', 'this is between Me and My servant', and 'My servant shall have what he asked'.

outline.heading: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz waits for the answer
outline.gist: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz paused after each verse of Al-Fatiha; asked why, he said he was picturing his Lord's reply.

outline.heading: He faces you as long as you face Him
outline.gist: Allah faces the servant who stands in prayer and responds as he speaks; the moment something else becomes more important in the heart, Allah turns away, but as long as you are focused on Him He is focused on you.

outline.heading: When the heart overflows, the tongue stumbles
outline.gist: He closes with something he has witnessed over twenty-five years: so much can come onto a worshipper's heart in the standing that his tongue stumbles from its abundance.

outline.heading: Interlude
The standing, the movement most worth contemplating
outline.gist: He returns to the standing as the part of the prayer he considers most worthy of reflection.

outline.heading: Ibn Mas'ud joins the Prophet's night prayer
outline.gist: The Prophet and companions found such joy in standing that their stories make it seem all they did; Ibn Mas'ud found the Prophet praying alone one night, joined him expecting a short prayer, and heard him begin Al-Baqarah.

outline.heading: The verse that made the Prophet weep
outline.gist: When Ibn Mas'ud recited An-Nisa to him and reached the verse about bringing a witness from every nation, the Prophet told him to stop, his eyes flowing with tears.

outline.heading: A hundred verses, then past them
outline.gist: In one rakah the Prophet went past a hundred verses, finished Al-Baqarah, then recited An-Nisa and Aal-Imran, until his companion was tempted to sit down and leave him.

outline.heading: Pausing at Paradise and the Fire
outline.gist: He recited unhurriedly, stopping at a mention of the Fire to seek refuge and at a mention of Paradise to ask for it, living the Quran as he prayed.

outline.heading: Bowing: taking the knee
outline.gist: Bowing was long the sign of admitting someone's superiority; taking the knee means accepting that the one before you is greater and that you are not his equal.

outline.heading: What is said in ruku
outline.gist: Ruku is for magnifying the Lord with the Prophet's words, such as glorifying the Lord of the angels and the Spirit and the dua offering one's hearing, sight, mind and bones in submission.

outline.heading: Interlude
Outro
